newsitem.title: INDIA: Snap polls loom as India coalition refuses talks.
newsitem.headline: Snap polls loom as India coalition refuses talks.

text.p: India's defeated United Front coalition on Saturday refused to join the nation's two other main blocs in talks to form a new government and a senior official said fresh polls seemed almost certain.

In a day of fast-changing plans, the caretaker alliance of ousted prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda first said it wanted to form a new power-sharing agreement with the Congress Party to avert a mid-term election. But their resolve appeared to be waning even before they could start talks with each other.

Deve Gowda was soundly defeated in a vote of confidence in parliament late on Friday, and immediately submitted the resignation of his 10-month-old centre-left government to President Shankar Dayal Sharma.
The confidence vote was triggered after the Congress Party, the 542-member parliament's third largest bloc, withdrew its make-or-break support for Deve-Gowda's minority coalition on March 30.
"The first priority is to avoid elections," Congress party president Sitaram Kesri told Reuters earlier in the day.
But a senior United Front official, speaking after the alliance leaders met Deve Gowda to probe the possibility of a new government, said elections looked inevitable.
"Dissolution of the Lok Sabha (lower house of parliament) is almost certain," said the official, who asked not to be named.
It was not clear what triggered the alliance's decision to consider elections as the only option.

The official's remark followed the United Front's decision not to support possible bids by either a Congress-led coalition or the right-wing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) to stake claims to establishing a new government.
"We will give a letter to the president on this issue," Railway Minister Ram Vilas Paswan said after the meeting.
President Sharma asked Deve Gowda to remain as caretaker prime minister while efforts were made to forge a new governing majority in the hung parliament.

Sharma has asked the parliament to meet on April 21 for three days to consider the budget for the 1997/98 (April-March) financial year, giving politicians until then to resolve their differences over a new government.

The budget plan, which would cut corporate and personal income taxes, has been held hostage to the two-week-old political crisis. Political leaders said there was a strong consensus in favour of approving the budget, but that it would be open to amendment.
Earlier, Kesri had said he wanted to stake a claim to form a fresh government.
However, when asked on Saturday if he would ask the president for the right to forge a new majority, Kesri said: "That is not the most important issue."

In a sign of the changed circumstances since Friday's vote of confidence, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram abandoned his chauffeur-driven official car and arrived at the meeting behind the wheel of his small sedan.
The common desire to avert elections stemmed from the shared conviction that the second polls in a year would only strengthen the hand of the BJP.

The rightwing party is the largest single group in the 542-member lower house with 162 votes, and held power for 12 days last May before it resigned in the face of certain defeat in a confidence vote.

The BJP has said it would stake a new claim to power only if it were able to muster a majority -- an unlikely prospect given the aversion in the United Front and Congress camps to allying with the Hindu nationalist party.
But fresh elections could put the BJP within striking distance of a majority, according to a recent opinion survey.
With Deve Gowda out of power except in a caretaker capacity, some politicians were expecting an easing of tension between Congress and the United Front.
But it was not clear whether they could dispel the acrimony that has built up over the past two weeks and settle on a common candidate and political programme to avert new elections.
